prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at that angle, which opened the field of moire quantum matter

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as my preferred single-part prize, with Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero. The first round did not change the science: a 2011 continuum-model prediction that a purely geometric parameter flattens the bands, a 2018 experiment that found correlated insulators and superconductivity in devices built at that angle, and rapid reproduction in many laboratories and in twisted multilayers and other moire systems. This is a discovery with identifiable originators, which is the test I applied in my own lecture remarks about a discovery or invention rather than lifetime achievement. The round also sharpened what I think is the real question. The chair asks whether the open pairing mechanism and the omission of Cao and Dean are reasons to wait or open questions inside a durable field. I judge them the second. The existence of the flat-band correlated states is not in dispute, and what a prize needs is a robust discovery, not a finished interpretation. I would write the citation around the prediction and the observation of the correlated states, not around the superconductivity mechanism and not around individual leadership, so that it does not imply the group leader alone made the experimental discovery. Of the four camps, this is the only one where theory and experiment each have a clean, uncontested originator. B020 has the strongest science but, as colleagues showed, four names competing for three seats with no agreed rule. B013 has clean names but is narrower as a discovery. B001 is the most mature but needs a five-to-three cut.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains maturity. The experiments are eight years old, the pairing mechanism is unsettled, the phase diagram depends on the sample, and three colleagues (Danielsson, Mehlig, Johansson) say a wait would cost little. I cannot dismiss that. The attribution gap is also real: Yuan Cao as first author, Cory Dean and others on hBN-encapsulated devices, and other early moire band-structure theorists are outside the credited names. Eriksson calls this a fairness problem that weakens the case this year, and I accept that a citation cannot repair it. I also concede that if the committee decides it cannot tolerate this gap, B001 is the safer choice on maturity, and I would not oppose it, but its cut among Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger and Zoller is no cleaner than the gap I am accepting here.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B001 first and B041 second, and argues that the unsettled pairing mechanism and the omitted experimentalists justify a modest wait, whereas the optical-lattice trio is easier to defend.
responses.response: I agree that B001 is the more settled field and that your trio of Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger is the cleanest experimental version of it. Where we differ is the bar. The pairing mechanism concerns what explains one derived phase; it does not make the discovery of flat-band correlated states uncertain, and earlier prizes have honoured discoveries whose full theory came later. I also point out that your own case against B001 concedes that Zoller and Cirac are excluded and that priority among Greiner, Bloch and Esslinger on the first Mott and fermionic results is intertwined. That is a contested attribution of the same weight as my Cao and Dean problem, so I do not think it tips the balance toward B001 on attribution. I have not changed my view, but your argument is the main reason B001 remains my first alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B041 first but says the missing first-author experimentalist is a fairness problem that the shortlist cannot repair and that it weakens the case for a prize this year.
responses.response: The chair asked the two of us to address this directly. I take your point more seriously than I did in round 1, and I disagree with only part of it. The omission of Cao and Dean is a real cost, but it comes from the three-person limit and from the fact that the experimental group leader conceived and directed the 2018 work, not from a defect in the discovery. I would therefore keep Jarillo-Herrero, and write a citation about the observed correlated states at the predicted angle, so that it does not claim he alone found them, and I would ask that the committee's background document name the Cao and device-quality contributions explicitly. I do not agree that this should delay the prize a year; waiting does not repair the credit, since the three-name constraint will still apply.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, ranks B020 first and proposes Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee as the founding leaders, arguing that for a detector-driven discovery the conception and construction of the instrument is the scientific contribution.
responses.response: I accept that the Higgs observation is the most important single result on the shortlist and fully mature, and I do not dispute your argument that instrument conception is a scientific contribution. My difficulty is not the science but the rule for credit. You propose Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee, Danielsson proposes Gianotti, Della Negra and Jenni, and colleagues disagree on whether construction or leadership at the announcement decides. The chair's own question asks for a principled rule and I do not see one that survives the three-name limit and names both ATLAS and CMS without leaving out someone with an equal claim. As an experimentalist I know that an instrument builder deserves credit, but I need the citation to say who did what. For B041 the citation can do that. This is why I rank B020 below B041 even though I accept that its science is the strongest on the list.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B020 first, calls the attribution a problem of how to credit and not of whether the discovery deserves it, and ranks B041 third as a discovery-then-explanation sequence.
responses.response: I agree the attribution problem for B020 is one of method, not merit, and you are candid that it is not resolved. But a prize cannot go out with the credit unresolved, because the citation is the decision. If the committee can settle on one rule, for example the founding spokespersons and project leaders, and one pair of names for each experiment, I would reconsider, and I say so openly. I also thank you for rating B041 as the sort of sequence the committee values; on your concern about the pairing mechanism, my answer is the one above, that the discovery stands whatever the mechanism turns out to be.

responses.point: Lindroth says the open pairing mechanism and the missing first-author experimentalist are the reasons to wait on B041, whereas the lattice-clock interpretation is stable.
responses.response: I accept that the clock case has the more settled interpretation and the cleaner two-name credit, and that is why B013 is my second alternative. I disagree that interpretive stability is the right test across fields. The clock result is a precision achievement whose physics was understood in advance, while the moire result is a discovery that could not have been predicted from the older literature, apart from the Bistritzer-MacDonald calculation. If the committee judges the prize to be for a discovery rather than a measurement advance, which is my reading of the criterion, B041 is the better fit. I would not oppose the clocks if the committee wants the more conservative choice.

responses.point: Johansson moved from B011 to B001 and now proposes Bloch, Greiner and Zoller, arguing that Cirac and Zoller should not be rewarded twice and that B001 and B011 should be one family.
responses.response: I share your view that the same people should not be rewarded across two parts, and for that reason I do not propose a two-part configuration: no second part fits within three people in total alongside the B041 trio. I respect the move to a mixed trio, but it is a different prize from Mehlig's, and as you note it leaves Esslinger out of an otherwise experimental case, so I read the camp as having two incompatible citations. I also noted in round 1 that I do not rely on your view of B008 because we are colleagues at Chalmers; I make no judgement on B001 that depends on you.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the unresolved pairing mechanism and sample dependence as a reason to wait or as an open question inside a durable field.
Whether the omission of Cao, Dean and other early experimentalists can be handled adequately in the citation and background material, or whether it is a decisive fairness problem.
Whether the committee will prefer maturity and a settled attribution (B001 or B013) to a younger but cleaner theory-then-experiment discovery.
I rely on memory for priority details and have not independently verified them.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict for B041 or for the alternatives B001 and B013 from my profile. I am an electron-microscopy and materials physicist at Chalmers with no documented link to MacDonald, Bistritzer or Jarillo-Herrero, nor to the cold-atom or clock candidates. Johansson is a Chalmers colleague and works in circuit QED (B008); I did not rely on his view of that candidate and have not changed that in round 2.
